title: Montaukett Indian Museum
summary: A museum at Second House in Montauk, where collections, contested authority over Native history, and Native leadership meet. David Bunn Martine’s appointment as director was reported in October 2026.
address_label: Second House grounds, 12 Second House Road, Montauk, NY
ancestral_territory_note: Public museum on Montaukett ancestral land; operated by the Montauk Historical Society.
why_this_matters: Native people are more than the subjects of museum displays. This place connects the history of collecting with ongoing questions of consent, interpretation, and community authority. Martine’s leadership offers visitors a way to encounter Montaukett continuity through a Native artist and museum professional, while the institution’s earlier debates remain part of its history.
introduction_title: A museum within a living Montaukett homeland
introduction_content:
The Montaukett Indian Museum stands on the Second House grounds in Montauk, near Fort Pond, within a homeland whose Native history continues through living families. Operated by the Montauk Historical Society, the museum presents Native history to residents and visitors. Its story also raises a question that collections alone cannot answer: who has authority to tell a people’s history?

The society’s current museum page reports that it has reviewed its inventory and reopened. Check that page for visiting information; exhibitions and seasonal access can change.
history_title: From collector-led project to Native leadership
history_content:
Lawrence Cooke began developing the museum project in 2001; it opened in 2017. The initiative emerged through the historical society and private collecting rather than as a tribally governed museum. Its leadership was contested: Robert Straight Arrow Cooper objected to Cooke leading it, while Cooke reported support from Robert Pharaoh. These different positions should not be reduced to a claim that all Montaukett people either supported or opposed the project. Source: Denis Hartnett, August 1, 2024.

On October 1, 2026, The East Hampton Star reported David Bunn Martine’s appointment as director. Martine, of Shinnecock, Montaukett, Apache, and Hungarian descent, brought more than twenty years of collections and exhibition work at the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum. He described adding personal artifacts and illustrations to make Montaukett life more visible. His emphasis was continuity: “we are still here.” Native leadership changes who interprets the collections; the appointment does not itself establish a transfer of the institution to tribal governance. Source: Christopher Walsh, October 1, 2026.
preservation_content: The museum stayed closed in summer 2024 while the society reconsidered its displays following new federal repatriation rules. Montaukett representative Sandi Brewster-walker requested an inventory before consultation. Cooke said the museum held no human remains or funerary objects; the closure should not be described as proof that it did. The dispute concerns both care for cultural belongings and Native authority over their interpretation. Source: “Montauk Indian Museum Is in Flux,” August 1, 2024.
artifacts_content:
Early plans drew on Lawrence Cooke’s collection and other private collections. They described photographs, stone tools, projectile points, hammerstones, and pottery fragments, with material from across Long Island rather than Montauk alone. These are records of Native skill and everyday life, but their routes into private collections also matter. An object’s place of origin and the circumstances of its collection should remain part of its interpretation. Source: “Indian Museum Taking Shape,” The East Hampton Star.

In February 2024, the society described stone tools, an educational mural, and replicas including a wampum belt and dugout canoe among the museum and Lighthouse displays. Replicas should be understood as teaching materials, distinct from original cultural belongings. This was an account of the displays at that time, not an inventory of everything currently on view. Source: Christine Sampson, February 15, 2024.
